questions.prompt: How many phone numbers are crammed into this one cell?
questions.explanation: Two values in one cell — exactly what 1NF forbids.

questions.prompt: Which normal form does product_name violate?
options: 2NF — it depends on only part of the key
questions.explanation: The key is (order_id, product_id) but product_name needs only product_id — partial dependency.

questions.prompt: Order the normal forms from weakest to strongest.
tax_rate depends on customer_id through city — a ___ dependency.
questions.explanation: A depends on B depends on C = transitive — 3NF's target.

questions.prompt: Match each normal form to its rule.

pairs.definition: No partial dependency on part of the key
No transitive dependency via another column

questions.prompt: This split — which JavaScript models it?
questions.code:
-- split repeating customer data out of Orders
CREATE TABLE Customers (customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY, phone TEXT);
options:
const customers = [{ customer_id: 1, phone: "555-01" }];
const orders = [{ order_id: 101, customer_id: 1 }];
questions.explanation: Customers live once in their own array; orders just hold the key.

questions.prompt: How many distinct phones are stored across these redundant rows?
questions.explanation: One real phone number stored twice — the redundancy normalization removes.

questions.prompt: Which normal form is violated? (city determines taxRate, neither is the key)
questions.code:
const customer = { id: 7, city: "Calgary", taxRate: 0.05 };
// taxRate depends on city, not on id
questions.explanation: taxRate depends on city (a non-key column), not directly on the key — classic 3NF violation.

questions.prompt: A key with more than one column is a ___ key — and only this kind makes 2NF relevant.
questions.explanation: Partial dependency needs a composite key to be partial on — single-column keys can't violate 2NF.

questions.prompt: Which SQL table design matches this 1NF shape?
options: CREATE TABLE Phones (customer_id INT, phone1 TEXT, phone2 TEXT);
questions.explanation: One value per cell, one phone per row — repeating groups become rows, not columns.
